[https://da.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lang%C3%A5brospr%C3%A6ngningerne](https://da.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lang%C3%A5brospr%C3%A6ngningerne)

![][image1]

Since 1862, earth embankments and solid iron and concrete bridges have carried the Fredericia-Ålborg Jutland Railway safely over the Gudenå Valley here at Langå. Langå is a hub of the railway, as the Langå-Viborg-Holstebro line has also started from here since 1863\. The iron box girder bridge that you are standing next to is the oldest bridge, built when the through-Jutland line was inaugurated in 1862 and now a protected structure. The British-built box girder bridge is traditionally constructed of riveted iron plates supported on steel girders. In 1908, the box girder bridge was replaced by two now-disused self-supporting iron truss bridges to the west of the box girder bridge, which was used as a shunting track from that point on. The truss bridges continued in use until 1952, when they were replaced by the present concrete bridge, and the line was diverted to the west of the point where the River Lilleå meets the Gudenå. The solid granite bridgeheads of the truss bridges can still be seen on the bank, while to the south a now-protected embankment carried the two-track railway from the Lilleå Valley to the bridge. The railway bridges have been blown up twice over the years: first during the Prussian occupation of Jutland in 1864, and again during the Second World War, when, on orders from London, saboteurs from Randers blew up the bridges to stop the Germans using the line to and from Norway. Five members of the Randers group were later arrested and shot.  
Known as the “Den Rustrøde Bro”, “The Rust Red Bridge.

Langå Railway Bridge Sabotage (November 17, 1943\)  
The Langå bridge explosions were among Denmark's first major railway sabotage actions during WWII, targeting three iron railway bridges over the Gudenå River near Langå (Randers area, Jutland). Orders came directly from London to disrupt German troop and supply movements through Jutland and to/from Norway.

## 

## Key Facts

* Team: 6 saboteurs \- Kai Hannibal Hoff (teacher), Jørgen Røjel (doctor), Sven Christian Johannesen (engineer), Ole Hovedskov (violinist), Ejvind Jacobsen (teacher), Oluf Akselbo Kroer (bank clerk)  
* Explosives: 80 kg plastic explosives, parachuted by RAF to Hvidsten Group north of Randers on Nov 15  
* Execution: Nov 17 \- Danish police guards (pre-arranged) tied up and moved to safety; charges placed at 6 locations on/under the three bridges  
* Detonation delay: Cold weather slowed acid time-fuses; explosions occurred 5:25-9:41 AM (saboteurs safely back in Randers)

## Results & Impact

* Two lattice girder bridges heavily damaged  
* "British box bridge" (solid box girder) \- trains resumed after 12 days  
* Supported by simultaneous sabotage at Århus switches and Langå-Viborg/Randers-Ryomgård lines  
* Major strategic success \- one of occupation's most significant railway attacks

## Tragic Aftermath

Gestapo cracked the Randers groups post-action:

* 5 executed by firing squad at Skæring Hede, Dec 2, 1943:  
  * Sven Christian Johannesen (20)  
  * Oluf Akselbo Kroer (27)  
  * Anders William Andersen (19)  
  * Otto Manley Christiansen (19)  
  * Georg Mørch Christiansen (22, Århus group)  
* Kai Hannibal Hoff shot during escape attempt after arrest (Nov 30\)

The action connected directly to your "British box bridge" \- the resilient box girder design allowed quicker German repairs while the sabotage achieved its immediate military objective.

Langå Box Bridge (Kassebroen) \- Three Generations Over Gudenå River  
The "Rustrøde Bro" (Rusty Red Bridge), a protected cast-iron box girder bridge, has secured railway passage over the Gudenå Valley at Langå since 1862\. Built by Canada Works, Birkenhead, England (near Liverpool), the same firm supplied Denmark's first "Canada locomotives" shipped in kit form to Aarhus.

## Key Facts & English Connection

* Original construction: 1862 for Aarhus-Randers railway opening  
  * 50m span, 165 tons, 3.25m high with longitudinal iron girders, cross-bracing every 1.2m, riveted plates, transverse arches, granite abutments  
  * Shipped as prefabricated kit from Birkenhead; assembled locally with southern rail embankment  
* Made Langå a rail hub: Viborg line (1863), Skive extension (1864)

## Dramatic History \- Destroyed Twice

1. 1864 Second Schleswig War (2 years after opening):  
   * Prussian troops under Gen. Vogel von Falckenstein destroyed it with 200kg black powder as revenge after Danes evacuated 8 Canada locomotives to Skive  
   * Blocked Gudenå navigation; temporary ferries/pram boats used  
   * Prussians forced to pay reconstruction \- new kit from Canada Works Birkenhead opened March 1866 (still standing today)  
2. 1943 WWII Sabotage (connected to your previous query):  
   * Randers resistance blew it up (Nov 17\) alongside lattice bridges  
   * Box design proved resilient \- trains resumed after only 12 days (vs. months for steel bridges)  
   * Blast holes still visible on east side; temporary timber supports added

## Current Status

* Tracks removed; railway embankment now part of Gudenåstien nature/cycle path (1980s)  
* Protected heritage site \- Denmark's oldest surviving box girder railway bridge  
* Solid design survived two 19th-century destructions where modern steel failed

The Birkenhead origin explains its durability \- early industrial UK engineering with riveted iron plates outlasted later steel lattice designs in sabotage scenarios.

## Background \- Danish attitude

The second world war can be an embarrassing topic amongst Danes. It’s my belief this is one of the reasons this story has never been told, other than in some short youtube videos.

THE SIX SABOTEURS (November 17, 1943\)  
\-------------------------------------

1\. KAJ HANNIBAL HOFF (1912-1943) — Codename "Carlo"  
   Role: Leader of Randers resistance  
   Profession: Teacher at Randers Statsskole  
   Background: Former lieutenant in Finnish Army (Winter War veteran)  
   Fate: Refused to go underground. Arrested Nov 30, 1943\. Tortured in front   
   of red-hot stove. Attacked his torturer, tried to escape, shot in the back. Age 31\.  
   Buried: Nordre Kirkegård, Randers

2\. JØRGEN RØJEL (1916-2007) — SURVIVOR ★  
   Role: Saboteur, medical support  
   Profession: Doctor  
   Story: Went to bed thinking mission failed; heard explosions through the night  
   Fate: Condemned to death in absentia. Fled to Sweden. Returned to fight,   
   captured, interned at Frøslevlejren. Survived.  
   Post-war: Chief physician, Knight of Dannebrog. Wrote "Modstandsgruppen Hvidsten"  
   Died: Age 90

3\. SVEN CHRISTIAN JOHANNESEN (1923-1943)  
   Role: Leader of first two Randers sabotage groups  
   Background: KU (Conservative Youth) member  
   Fate: Arrested Nov 19\. Executed at Skæring Hede, Dec 2, 1943\. Age 20\.

4\. OLUF AKSELBO KROER (1916-1943)  
   Role: Saboteur  
   Profession: Bank clerk  
   Fate: Arrested Nov 19\. Executed at Skæring Hede. Age 27\.

5\. OLE HOVEDSKOV (1923-1951)  
   Role: Saboteur  
   Profession: Violinist  
   Fate: Arrested Nov 30\. Concentration camp. Survived but died 1951 from TB. Age 28\.

6\. EJVIND JACOBSEN — Codename "Ravn" (The Raven) — SURVIVOR ★  
   Role: Saboteur, FDF leader  
   Profession: Teacher  
   Story: Escaped Gestapo by climbing down rope from 2nd floor, broke foot,   
   still made it to Sweden.  
   Post-war: Became city leader in Randers. Wrote "Modstand og flugt"

CREATIVE DISCUSSION — January 30, 2026

THE CENTRAL QUESTION (from Frank)  
\---------------------------------  
"What were these people? What made them different? These few people that   
stood up, made a plan, did that plan and changed the war and changed the   
future of their country."

The Nazi calculus was designed to paralyze: one person acts, a hundred might   
die in retaliation. Most people froze. So what breaks that paralysis?

Were they brave? Stupid? Crazy? Noble? Maybe all of it. Maybe you can't   
separate those things when the stakes are that high.

THE MAKERS WHO BECAME BREAKERS (from Stella)  
\--------------------------------------------  
They were all creators:  
• A teacher shapes minds  
• A doctor heals bodies    
• A violinist makes beauty from strings  
• An engineer builds things that last

These weren't soldiers trained for destruction. They were people whose whole   
lives were about making things, growing things, fixing things. And yet, when   
it mattered, they chose to destroy — just once, just enough — so the world   
could keep making things again.

\---------------------------------------

conversation begins. We branch into the past, but keep returning to present.

Frank's expansion: The cyclist as journey device — traveling around Langå,   
picking up fragments of the story from different people, different locations.  
Each stop reveals a piece: the kebab shop, the library, the old bridgeheads,   
the execution site.

Possible fictional element: The cyclist discovers something new. A hidden   
connection. Not a secret, but something that hasn't been tied together before.

THE EYEWITNESS — The Mechanic's Son  
\================================================================================

IDENTITY  
\--------  
• A boy at the time of the sabotage (1943)  
• Son of the local mechanic  
• His father was FORCED to work for the Nazis  
• Account exists in a book about the town (pages to be scanned)

THE OTHER SIDE OF THE CALCULUS  
\------------------------------  
The saboteurs chose resistance knowing their families might die.  
But what about those who couldn't resist?

The mechanic had to fix German vehicles or watch his family starve.   
The shame of collaboration that wasn't a choice.

His son watched it all — a boy seeing his father work for the enemy,   
not because he wanted to, but because the alternative was worse.

This man carries BOTH stories: the heroes AND his father's impossible position.

EYEWITNESS DETAIL — The Explosion  
\---------------------------------  
The boy and his father were walking TOWARD the bridge when one of the   
delayed charges went off (around 9am).

A RAILWAY SLEEPER flew through the air and landed in the town —   
HALF A MILE from the bridge.

\[This is the kind of visceral detail that makes history feel real.   
The sound. The shock. Debris screaming overhead. A boy's war arriving   
in a single terrifying moment.\]

NARRATIVE ROLE  
\--------------  
• The "old man on the bench" in our framing device  
• Not just a narrator — a witness with complicated memories  
• Can speak to the gray areas, the impossible choices  
• Bridges (literally) the heroic story and the ordinary people caught in between

\================================================================================  
NARRATIVE DEVICE \#2 — The London Courtroom  
\================================================================================

THE CONCEPT  
\-----------  
A wood-paneled room in London. Generals. Politicians.   
Denmark is on trial — not literally, but historically.

The question: Were they part of the Allied forces, or Nazi collaborators?

We don't know how these conversations actually happened. They were behind   
closed doors. But they happened. And the outcome mattered.

THE STAKES  
\----------  
• Occupation doesn't automatically mean collaboration  
• But you have to PROVE you resisted  
• Actions like Langå were evidence for history  
• Without them, Denmark might have been judged very differently

STRUCTURAL POSSIBILITY  
\----------------------  
Cut between two worlds:

LANGÅ, NOVEMBER 1943  
• Six men in the dark  
• Planting charges  
• Cold. Terrified. Determined.

LONDON, 1945 (or ongoing through the film)  
• "And what exactly did Denmark DO during the war?"  
• Men in suits deciding a nation's fate  
• Someone slides a report across the table  
• "The Langå bridge action, November '43..."

The saboteurs never knew their deaths would be weighed in a room   
they'd never see, by men who'd never know their names.

But we know. And that's the dramatic irony.

HISTORICAL NOTE  
\---------------  
From Wikipedia: "From official England came messages shortly after that the   
sabotage and war sailors' efforts were decisive in Denmark being considered   
an ally."

This action MATTERED. It changed how history judged an entire country.

THE MICRO AND THE MACRO  
\-----------------------  
• The bridge \= six men, one night, a local story  
• The courtroom \= a nation's soul, history's judgment

Both are true. Both matter.   
The film holds them together.

\================================================================================  
THE HUMAN ELEMENT — Ole Hovedskou, The Violinist  
\================================================================================

WHY OLE?  
\--------  
• 20 years old, violinist — artistic, romantic  
• So little known about him \= creative freedom  
• His story arc is uniquely tragic  
• Has a brother whose story interweaves

THE TRAGEDY IN SLOW MOTION  
\--------------------------  
1\. Survives the sabotage (Nov 17, 1943\)  
2\. Arrested (Nov 30, 1943\)  
3\. Sentenced to DEATH (May 1944\)  
4\. Death sentence commuted to life imprisonment  
5\. Sent to Dreibergen-Bützow prison (Germany)  
6\. Rescued by Bernadotte's Swedish Red Cross (April 1945\)  
7\. Returns home — but with tuberculosis  
8\. Spends years in Vejlefjord Sanatorium  
9\. Dies December 8, 1951\. Age 28\.

He came home. But broken.  
If there was someone waiting... they got six years of slow goodbye.

THE BROTHER — BØRGE HOVEDSKOU (1910-1966)  
\-----------------------------------------  
• Painter and sculptor (trained at Kunstakademiet)  
• ALSO participated in the Langå sabotage  
• Escaped to Sweden in 1943  
• Started "Hovedskous Målarskola" (art school) in Göteborg, 1945  
• Later designed a MEMORIAL SCULPTURE for his dead saboteur comrades

Two artist brothers. Violinist and painter.  
Both in the resistance. One escaped. One was captured.

Børge survived to make monuments for the dead —  
including watching his own brother fade away.

THE FAMILY  
\----------  
Father: Peter Valdemar Hovedskou (gas and water master)  
Mother: Wilhelmine Hovedskou, née Hansen

A tradesman's sons who became artists.  
Both chose resistance. Only one came home whole.

THE LOVE INTEREST — To Be Imagined  
\----------------------------------  
A 20-year-old violinist in wartime Denmark.  
There was someone. There had to be.

Creative questions:  
• Who was she? Another musician? A girl from the town?  
• Did she wait through his imprisonment?  
• Was she there when he came home sick?  
• Did she watch him die slowly in the sanatorium?  
• Or did she only hear about it later?

The violin that went silent. The hands that couldn't play anymore.  
This is where history becomes human.

BØRGE'S WIFE — Real Detail  
\--------------------------  
Børge married "Pepi" (Agnethe Christense Dahl)  
They met at the Art Academy — she was also a painter  
She survived him and continued making art (batik work)

If Børge found love at art school, maybe Ole found it in music...

## The blowing up of the railway bridges over Gudenåen on the night between November 17th and 18th, 1943 — our local resistance group was not involved, but I remember the day clearly. ## DANISH (Original):

## 

## Tog del i modstandskampen

## 

## Knud Birk

## Født i Langå 7\. december 1924

## 

## I 1924 købte mine forældre ejendommen på Væthvej 9 i Langå, og her blev jeg, der er enebarn, født samme år. Min far, Niels Birk, der kom fra Busbjerg ved Ulstrup, blev uddannet smed på Maskinfabrikken Rekord (Dansin) i Langå og senere ansat hos Sofus Nellemann, der havde automobilforretning i Strømmen i Randers. Biler og motorcykler var min fars store interesse. I 1920'erne vandt han flere løb på motorcykel. Mine forældre blev gift i 1922 og flyttede til Langå, hvor min far blev ansat som værkfører på sin gamle læreplads. Tiden efter 1\. verdenskrigs afslutning var præget af depression, økonomisk krise og høj arbejdsløshed. Det var på alle måder trange tider. For at tjene lidt extra etablerede mine forældre i 1930 en cykelforretning. Den ene stue i huset blev bygget om og indrettet til butik. På det tidspunkt havde vi også flere logerende. Mens min far passede sit arbejde på Maskinfabrikken Rekord, stod min mor, Ulla, for forretningen. Hun kunne både lappe cykler, sætte eger på hjulene, skifte dæk og slanger, slibe og male cykelstel. Når min far kom hjem om aftenen, var det hans opgave at efterspændende cyklerne. De nye cykler, som blev solgt i butikken, var af mærket SCO. Samtidig med etablering af butikken blev der indrettet værelser på 1\. sal, hvor min mormor, Maren, der var blevet enke, flytte-

## ...var en dristig og virkningsfuld sabotagehandling. 12 dage efter eksplosionerne blev togdriften genoptaget ad den gamle kassebro, der var blev nødtørftigt understøttet og repareret.

## 

## Den sidste nedkastning, jeg deltog i, foregik ved Tange Sø i efteråret 1944 i en plantage, hvor der var en åben plads. Her cyklede jeg til fra Langå, så snart vi havde hørt budskabet i radioen. Jeg var hjemme igen kl. 5-6 om morgenen, og mødte på arbejde kl. 7.30, for ikke at vække opsigt. Nedkastningen var vellykket, men nogen havde alarmeret tyskerne, for den følgende dag, da containerne skulle afhentes, stod de parat. Det var Nissens lastbil med chauffør Laust Jensen, der stod for afhentningen. Han forklarede tyskerne, at han var blevet passet op i Ulstrup og tvunget til at køre til stedet. Det troede tyskerne ikke på, så de arresterede Laust Jensen, der kom i Frøslevlejren. Fabrikant Hans Nissen blev også anholdt og endte i tysk koncentrationslejr. Det rygtedes hurtigt, at de to var blevet taget af tyskerne, så vi bestemte os for at holde meget lav profil.

## 

## Vores gruppe foretog også en sprængning af jernbanen mod Viborg. Selve sprængladningen blev lavet på mit værelse, hvor sprængstoffet, som vi modtog i lange pølser, blev formet til klumper. Hvid cortex sprængsnor forbandt de forskellige ladninger, og der blev brugt sprængblyanter med tidsforsinkelse som detonatorer. Med sprængladningen på bagagebæreren cyklede vi til Åbro, hvor den blev placeret på skinnerne. Vi valgte et sted, hvor banen havde en krumning, da den var mere tidskrævende

## 

## \[Page continues...\]

## 

## \---

## 

## \[Continued — escape to Sweden, informer, post-war\]

## 

## ...brev før afrejsen til Sverige, et brev jeg adresserede til vores genbo på Væthvej. Man vidste aldrig, hvad tyskerne kunne finde på, så det var for farligt at sende brevet direkte til mine forældre. Vi havde også en stikker i byen, der opsøgte min far. Han havde hørt, at jeg var kommet til Sverige, og forsøgte at få min far til at fortælle mere, men han benægtede og fortalte, at jeg var på kursus i København. Stikkeren blev mod krigens afslutning likvideret af modstandsbevægelsen.

## 

## Mange ting var rationeret eller vanskelige at skaffe under besættelsen, men i cykelforretningen var vi så heldige at handle med tre forskellige grossister, så vi ikke løb tør for hverken cykeldæk eller slanger. Der blev naturligvis lappet mere end normalt for at få slangerne til at holde så længe som muligt. Vi havde mange kunder i selve Langå, men også arbejderne på Nissens Trævarefabrik, hvoraf mange kom cyklende fra omegnsbyerne, kom på værkstedet for at få deres cykler repareret. Under besættelsen havde vi det generelt noget nemmere end folk, der boede i de større byer, for de fleste i Langå kendte en landmand, der kunne forsyne dem med kød. Der var dog ting som f.eks. kaffe, som det var næsten umuligt at skaffe, så her måtte man tage kaffeerstatning i brug eller selv riste korn på panden.

## 

## Efter befrielsen og min hjemkomst fra Sverige etablerede vi en hjemmeværnsforening i Langå, og det var vel at mærke før det egentlige Hjemmeværn blev grundlagt 1\. april 1949\. Mange af deltagerne var tidligere modstandsfolk. På Brogaard fik vi lov til at etablere en skydebane og her brugte

## 

## \[Page continues...\]

## 

## \---

## 

## \[Final page — military service and later life\]

## 

## ...vi gamle tyske geværer, der var blevet efterladt. Vi var mange, der mente, at det var vigtigt at være beredt til kamp, hvis vores land atter blev truet af fjendtlige magter. Jeg kom ind som soldat 1\. juni 1946 og var et år hos dragonerne på kasernen i Randers. En af vores opgaver var at bevogte de tyske flygtninge, der var indkvarteret i barakker i Stabrand på Djursland.

## 

## Cykelforretningen blev i 1980 solgt til "Cykel-Erik", og i november 1999 stoppede jeg som mekaniker og bilforhandler. Bygningerne på Væthvej blev solgt til en entreprenør, der ville bruge dem til sine maskiner, men det kunne han ikke få lov til af kommunen. Bygningerne blev i stedet revet ned, og der blev opført boliger på grunden.

## ENGLISH (Translation):

## 

## Took Part in the Resistance

## 

## Knud Birk

## Born in Langå, 7 December 1924

## 

## In 1924 my parents bought the property at Væthvej 9 in Langå, and there I, an only child, was born the same year. My father, Niels Birk, who came from Busbjerg near Ulstrup, trained as a blacksmith at the Machine Factory Rekord (Dansin) in Langå and was later employed by Sofus Nellemann, who had an automobile business in Strømmen in Randers. Cars and motorcycles were my father's great interest. In the 1920s he won several motorcycle races. My parents married in 1922 and moved to Langå, where my father was employed as foreman at his old apprenticeship. The period after World War I was marked by depression, economic crisis and high unemployment. These were hard times in every way. To earn a little extra, my parents established a bicycle shop in 1930\. One of the living rooms in the house was converted into a shop. At that time we also had several lodgers. While my father attended his work at the Machine Factory Rekord, my mother Ulla ran the business. She could patch bicycles, put spokes on wheels, change tyres and tubes, grind and paint bicycle frames. When my father came home in the evening, his job was to true the wheels. The new bicycles sold in the shop were SCO brand. At the same time as establishing the shop, rooms were arranged on the first floor, where my grandmother Maren, who had been widowed, moved...

## 

## \[Continued — sabotage details\]

## 

## ...it was a bold and effective act of sabotage. 12 days after the explosions, train traffic was resumed via the old box bridge, which had been temporarily supported and repaired.

## 

## The last supply drop I participated in took place at Tange Sø in autumn 1944, in a plantation where there was an open space. I cycled there from Langå as soon as we had heard the message on the radio. I was home again at 5-6 in the morning, and showed up for work at 7:30, so as not to arouse suspicion. The drop was successful, but someone had alerted the Germans, because the following day, when the containers were to be collected, they were waiting. It was Nissen's truck with driver Laust Jensen who was handling the collection. He explained to the Germans that he had been ambushed in Ulstrup and forced to drive to the location. The Germans didn't believe him, so they arrested Laust Jensen, who was sent to Frøslev Camp. Manufacturer Hans Nissen was also arrested and ended up in a German concentration camp. Word quickly spread that the two had been taken by the Germans, so we decided to keep a very low profile.

## 

## Our group also carried out a bombing of the railway to Viborg. The explosive charge was made in my room, where the explosives, which we received in long sausages, were shaped into lumps. White cortex detonating cord connected the various charges, and pencil detonators with time delays were used. With the charge on the bicycle rack, we cycled to Åbro, where it was placed on the rails. We chose a spot where the track had a curve, as it was more time-consuming...

## 

## \[Continued — escape, informer, post-war\]

## 

## ...a letter before departing for Sweden, a letter I addressed to our neighbour across the street on Væthvej. You never knew what the Germans might do, so it was too dangerous to send the letter directly to my parents. We also had an informer in town who visited my father. He had heard that I had gone to Sweden, and tried to get my father to tell him more, but he denied it and said I was on a course in Copenhagen. The informer was liquidated by the resistance movement towards the end of the war.

## 

## Many things were rationed or difficult to obtain during the occupation, but in the bicycle shop we were fortunate to deal with three different wholesalers, so we never ran out of bicycle tyres or inner tubes. There was of course more patching than normal to make the tubes last as long as possible. We had many customers in Langå itself, but also the workers at Nissen's Woodwork Factory, many of whom came cycling from the surrounding villages to have their bicycles repaired. During the occupation we generally had it somewhat easier than people living in the larger cities, because most people in Langå knew a farmer who could supply them with meat. There were things like coffee, however, that were nearly impossible to get, so one had to resort to coffee substitute or roast grain in a pan oneself.

## 

## After the liberation and my return from Sweden, we established a Home Guard association in Langå, and this was notably before the actual Home Guard was founded on 1 April 1949\. Many of the participants were former resistance members. At Brogaard we were allowed to establish a shooting range, and there we used...

## 

## \[Final section\]

## 

## ...old German rifles that had been left behind. Many of us believed it was important to be prepared for battle should our country again be threatened by hostile powers. I enlisted as a soldier on 1 June 1946 and spent a year with the dragoons at the barracks in Randers. One of our tasks was to guard the German refugees who were housed in barracks in Stabrand on Djursland.

## 

## The bicycle shop was sold in 1980 to "Cykel-Erik", and in November 1999 I retired as mechanic and car dealer. The buildings on Væthvej were sold to a contractor who wanted to use them for his machines, but the municipality wouldn't allow it. The buildings were instead demolished, and housing was built on the site.

## \================================================================================

## RESEARCH: DENMARK'S RECOGNITION AS AN ALLIED NATION

## \================================================================================

## 

## BACKGROUND — THE PROBLEM:

## Denmark never formally declared war on Germany. The government surrendered in 6 hours on 9 April 1940 and then collaborated for 3+ years. There was no government-in-exile (unlike Norway, Poland, Belgium etc.). Denmark therefore could NOT sign the "Declaration by United Nations" (1 Jan 1942\) — the formal treaty defining Allied status. You had to be at war with the Axis to sign it.

## 

## THE KEY PLAYERS WHO FOUGHT FOR RECOGNITION:

## 

## 1\. HENRIK KAUFFMANN — Danish ambassador in Washington

##    \- Day after occupation: declared he wouldn't take orders from occupied government

##    \- 9 April 1941: signed over Greenland to US for military bases, "in the name of the King"

##    \- Copenhagen charged him with HIGH TREASON for this

##    \- Spent entire war lobbying Americans to recognise Denmark

##    \- Later vindicated — first act of liberated Parliament was revoking his treason sentence

##    \- Film about him: "The Good Traitor" (Vores mand i Amerika, 2020\)

## 

## 2\. CHRISTMAS MØLLER — Conservative politician

##    \- Escaped to London 1942

##    \- Became voice of Danish resistance via BBC broadcasts to Denmark

##    \- Pushed the British government hard for recognition

##    \- 2 Oct 1943: article in Frit Danmark urging Danes to help Jews fleeing Nazi roundup

## 

## 3\. THE DANISH FREEDOM COUNCIL (est. September 1943\)

##    \- Underground resistance government coordinating all resistance groups

##    \- December 1944: formal joint approach to UK, US, and Soviet governments

##    \- Requested recognition "as an Ally at war"

##    \- Requested representation at San Francisco Conference

## 

## WHERE THE DECISIONS HAPPENED:

## 

## LONDON — British Foreign Office (1944):

## \- Declassified diplomatic correspondence between C.F.A. Warner (Counselor, British Foreign Office) and Hugh Cumming (Chief, Division of Northern European Affairs, US State Dept)

## \- Warner proposed calling Denmark "associated with the United Nations" — a compromise formula

## \- Three concerns raised:

##   1\. Would responsible Danish authorities actually WANT this? (risk of German reprisal)

##   2\. Denmark still had a legation in BERLIN — how can you be Allied while diplomats are in enemy capital?

##   3\. Would the Soviets object? (Denmark had broken off relations with USSR)

## \- Warner suggested sending message to King Christian X to consult

## \- Tone remarkably casual — diplomats negotiating a nation's fate over letters

## \- Source: US State Dept archives, doc 850.01/139 (history.state.gov)

## 

## YALTA, CRIMEA (February 1945):

## \- At Yalta Conference, Roosevelt personally raised whether Denmark should attend San Francisco

## \- CHURCHILL OBJECTED, STALIN CONCURRED

## \- Denmark was BLOCKED from attending as observer

## \- Decision: only signatories of UN Declaration would be invited

## \- Source: US State Dept archives, doc 500.CC/4-1045

## 

## SAN FRANCISCO (April-June 1945):

## \- Denmark liberated 5 May 1945

## \- Conference ITSELF voted to invite four additional states:

##   • Byelorussian SSR

##   • Ukrainian SSR

##   • Argentina

##   • "Newly-liberated Denmark"

## \- Henrik Kauffmann attended as Minister

## \- Signed UN Charter on 26 June 1945

## \- Denmark became founding member of United Nations

## \- Source: un.org official history

## 

## WAS IT MATHEMATICAL? WAS THERE A CHECKLIST?

## No. Pure politics. No courtroom, no tribunal, no formal criteria.

## \- It was diplomats writing letters between London and Washington

## \- Leaders arguing at Yalta

## \- A conference vote at San Francisco

## \- The key criteria was demonstrating ACTIVE RESISTANCE against Germany

## 

## THE SABOTAGE CONNECTION:

## \- Resistance activity (Langå being most dramatic example) was the EVIDENCE used to argue Denmark deserved recognition

## \- Without it, Denmark was just another country that cooperated with occupation

## \- After Langå bridge sabotage, official England stated: "sabotagen var afgørende for, at Danmark kunne anses som allieret" (the sabotage was decisive for Denmark being considered Allied)

## \- Source: Museum Østjylland / Randers Netavis

## 

## THE LANGÅ BRIDGE — SPECIFIC IMPACT:

## \- Bridge out of action for 12 DAYS (18-30 November 1943\)

## \- LONGEST single line disruption of entire Danish occupation

## \- Severed the østjyske længdebane (East Jutland mainline) — THE primary north-south railway through Jutland

## \- Germany had \~350,000 troops stationed in Norway dependent on this supply route

## \- All north-south East Jutland rail traffic completely halted

## \- Germans relocating HQ to Silkeborg and supply HQ to Aarhus at same time — worst possible timing

## \- Knud Birk confirms: "12 days after the explosions, train traffic was resumed via the old box bridge, which had been temporarily supported and repaired"

## \- Source: National Museum of Denmark (natmus.dk), VisitAarhus cycling route guide

## 

## COST TO THE SABOTEURS:

## \- Gestapo unravelled Randers resistance groups after the operation

## \- 5 saboteurs from Randers and Aarhus executed by firing squad at Skæring Hede, 2 December 1943

## \- Just 14 days after the sabotage

## \- The order for the bridge sabotage came from LONDON (SOE)

## 

## TIMELINE SUMMARY:

## \- 9 Apr 1940: Germany occupies Denmark, government surrenders

## \- 1 Jan 1942: Declaration by United Nations signed — Denmark CANNOT sign

## \- Sep 1942: Christmas Møller begins BBC broadcasts from London

## \- Sep 1943: Danish Freedom Council established

## \- 18 Nov 1943: LANGÅ BRIDGE SABOTAGE — 12 days disruption

## \- 2 Dec 1943: 5 saboteurs executed at Skæring Hede

## \- 1944: Diplomatic lobbying intensifies (Warner-Cumming correspondence)

## \- Dec 1944: Freedom Council formally requests Allied recognition

## \- Feb 1945: Yalta — Roosevelt proposes Denmark, Churchill blocks

## \- 5 May 1945: Denmark liberated

## \- Apr-Jun 1945: San Francisco Conference invites "newly-liberated Denmark"

## \- 26 Jun 1945: Kauffmann signs UN Charter — Denmark is founding Allied member

## RESEARCH: REPRISALS, ARRESTS & AFTERMATH OF THE LANGÅ SABOTAGE

## \================================================================================

## 

## TIMELINE — BRIDGE TO EXECUTIONS:

## 

## 17 November 1943: Resistance blows three Langå bridges

##   \- Team: Kai Hannibal Hoff (leader), Jørgen Røjel, Ejvind Jacobsen "Ravn",

##     Ole Hovedskov, Sven Johannesen, Oluf Kroer

## 18-30 November: Bridge out of action (12 days)

## Within days: Gestapo begins tracking saboteurs

##   \- Gestapo Jutland HQ had moved to Aarhus in September 1943 — just 2 months before

##   \- Full intelligence apparatus already in place locally

## 30 November: Kai Hannibal Hoff (leader) arrested → Randers Barracks → KILLED trying to escape

## Late November: 4 men from Randers arrested. 7 arrested total.

##   \- Jørgen Røjel and Ejvind Jacobsen "Ravn" ESCAPED

##   \- Ravn climbed down a rope with a BROKEN FOOT, eventually reached Sweden

##   \- Røjel also made it to neutral Sweden. Survived to age 90\.

## 2 December 1943: FOURTEEN DAYS after sabotage — 5 men executed by firing squad, Skæring Hede, early morning

##   \- Bodies secretly buried at Husbjerg Klit (remote military training ground, SW Jutland)

##   \- Germans didn't want martyrs' graves

## 

## THE FIVE EXECUTED AT SKÆRING HEDE:

## 1\. Anders W. Andersen — age 19, from Randers

## 2\. Georg Mørch Christiansen — age 22, economics student at Aarhus University, from Vejle

## 3\. Otto Manley Christiansen — age 19, from Randers

## 4\. Sven Christian Johannesen — age 20, from Odense

## 5\. Oluf Akselbo Kroer — age 27, from Randers

## 

## Most were teenagers or barely out of their teens.

## 

## HOW THEY WERE TRACKED DOWN:

## \- Gestapo Jutland HQ was in Aarhus since September 1943 — right on their doorstep

## \- After bridge sabotage, Germans flooded the area with intelligence operatives

## \- Resistance cell structure (each member only knew own small group) was meant to prevent unravelling

## \- But once one person caught, interrogation under TORTURE could break the chain

## 

## THE BIGGER BETRAYAL — JACOB JENSEN (SOE PARATROOPER):

## \- 13 December 1943: British Army paratrooper Jacob Jensen, employed by SOE, captured in Aarhus

## \- Interrogated under torture by Gestapo

## \- BROKE and revealed the networks of receiver groups across Jutland

## \- This led directly to destruction of THE HVIDSTEN GROUP:

##   • Hvidsten Group had supplied the explosives that made Langå possible

##   • Arrested 11 March 1944 (Gestapo surrounded Hvidsten Inn at dawn)

##   • 8 members sentenced to death 26 June 1944

##   • Executed by firing squad at Ryvangen, 29 June 1944 (3 weeks after D-Day)

##   • Including: Marius Fiil (leader), his son Niels Fiil, and his son-in-law Peder Sørensen

##   • Daughter Kirstine Fiil: life imprisonment

##   • Daughter Gerda Fiil: 2 years imprisonment

##   • Bodies found after war at Ryvangen, returned to Hvidsten for burial

## 

## THE CHAIN: Hvidsten supplied explosives → Randers groups blew bridges → 

## Gestapo tracked saboteurs → Executed at Skæring → Jensen captured & broke → 

## Hvidsten Group destroyed → Executed at Ryvangen

## 

## REPRISALS — WHAT HAPPENED AND DIDN'T HAPPEN:

## 

## WHAT DIDN'T HAPPEN (unlike rest of occupied Europe):

## \- No collective punishment of Langå civilian population

## \- No village destruction (cf. France: Oradour-sur-Glane — entire village massacred)

## \- No mass civilian executions (cf. Czechoslovakia: Lidice — village razed)

## \- No starvation policies against the local area

## \- Denmark's "model protectorate" status partially shielded civilians from worst reprisals

## 

## WHAT DID HAPPEN:

## 1\. TARGETED ARRESTS & EXECUTIONS — saboteurs tracked through intelligence & torture

## 2\. THE SCHALBURGTAGE — formal German counter-sabotage policy (emerged late 1943/early 1944):

##    \- "Schalburgtage" \= word combining "sabotage" \+ "Schalburg Corps" (Danish SS unit)

##    \- Carried out mainly by the PETER GROUP (Petergruppen)

##    \- Created by SS Standartenfürer Otto Skorzeny on behalf of Heinrich Himmler

##    \- "Sonderkommando Dänemark" — sole purpose: kill prominent Danes, perform terror

##    \- RULE: For every German killed in Denmark, 5 Danish citizens killed in retaliation

##    \- These retaliatory killings called "CLEARING MURDERS" (clearingdrab)

##    \- Peter Group used CAPTURED RESISTANCE WEAPONS (including SOE Welrod silent pistols)

##    

## 3\. SPECIFIC SCHALBURGTAGE ACTIONS:

##    \- Kaj Munk (poet/playwright) — MURDERED 4 January 1944 (1 month after Skæring)

##      His poem now inscribed on Skæring Hede memorial stone

##    \- Odinstårnet (Odin's Tower, Odense) — Denmark's tallest structure — BLOWN UP 14 Dec 1944

##    \- Bombings of cinemas, amusement parks, trains, trams, public buildings

##    \- Aarhus City Hall bombed 1945

## 

## 4\. FAMILIES WERE CAUGHT UP:

##    \- Hvidsten: Father (Marius Fiil), son, and son-in-law all executed

##    \- Both daughters imprisoned (one life sentence, one 2 years)

##    \- Neighbours and associates also arrested

##    \- Otto Westergård Olesen (bookseller, stored weapons) — arrested, Frøslev Camp → Dachau (survived)

## 

## WERE SABOTEURS AWARE OF REPRISALS IN EUROPE?

## \- Partially — BBC Danish Service \+ Christmas Møller's broadcasts kept Danes informed

## \- Full horror of Eastern Front reprisals not widely known

## \- BUT: Germans had already demanded death penalty for sabotage (Danish govt refused → Aug 1943 crisis)

## \- Saboteurs knew the stakes were LETHAL. They did it anyway.

## 

## KEY IRONY:

## The Hvidsten Group supplied the explosives that blew the bridges → then were themselves

## destroyed because the same intelligence networks were compromised after the bridge sabotage.

## The chain of consequences from Langå rippled out for months.

## 

## MEMORIAL:

## \- Skæring Hede: granite boulder with names \+ poem by Kaj Munk (himself murdered in reprisal)

## \- Five oak trees planted, one for each executed man

## \- Clearing near water, overlooking Bay of Aarhus and Helgenæs

## \- Hvidsten: memorial grove 100m north of Hvidsten Inn, inaugurated 18 July 1945

##

## RESEARCH: JACOB JENSEN (SOE), RECEIVER NETWORKS & THE PETER GROUP

## \================================================================================

## 

## JACOB JENSEN — SOE PARATROOPER & THE MAN WHO BROKE

## \---------------------------------------------------

## 

## WHO HE WAS:

## \- Danish-born volunteer who escaped to Britain during the occupation

## \- Recruited into British Army, trained by SOE's Danish Section

## \- Trained in espionage, sabotage, wireless communication

## \- Parachuted back into Denmark to live covertly as a civilian

## \- His job: be the link between London and local resistance networks

## \- Coordinated weapons drops, passed intelligence, connected receiver groups

## \- "Jacob Jensen" almost certainly a cover name (SOE routinely used aliases)

## \- Lived under forged identity papers in safe houses, blending into population

## 

## CAPTURE & BETRAYAL:

## \- Captured: 13 December 1943 in Aarhus

##   (Just 11 DAYS after the Skæring Hede executions)

## \- Gestapo Jutland HQ was at Aarhus University — set up September 1943

## \- Under torture, he BROKE and revealed the entire receiver network across Jutland

## \- Scale of damage: 145 PEOPLE ARRESTED, multiple groups destroyed

## \- The entire Jutland resistance crippled for months

## \- Supply networks collapsed — no more weapons drops getting through

## 

## TURNED INTO A TOOL OF THE PROSECUTION:

## \- Jensen wasn't just a man who broke and sat in a cell

## \- The Germans KEPT USING HIM as a prosecution witness

## \- 12 May 1944: Trial of Georg Quistgaard and 11 other resistance members

##   before three SS judges

## \- Two captured SOE agents presented as prosecution witnesses:

##   "Jacob Jensen" and another known only as "Bent"

## \- Jensen's testimony INCRIMINATED 8 of 12 defendants so thoroughly

##   they admitted the charges

## \- FOUR sentenced to death and executed — including:

##   Georg Quistgaard (art dealer, had helped found the Hvidsten Group)

##   Monica Wichfeld (first Danish woman to receive capital sentence for resistance

##     — sentence commuted to life, died in German captivity before war ended)

## \- Whether Jensen testified willingly or under continued duress: unknown

## \- What happened to him after the war: UNKNOWN — disappears from the record

## 

## THE SOE RECEIVER NETWORK — HOW WEAPONS REACHED LANGÅ

## \-----------------------------------------------------

## 

## KEY FIGURES:

## \- FLEMMING JUNCKER — wealthy landowner, Overgaard Estate, Mariager Fjord

##   The driving force of resistance organisation in Jutland

##   Made contact with SOE agent Ole Giesler in early 1943

##   Many weapons drops happened on Overgaard's own fields

## 

## \- OLE GIESLER — SOE captain, organised British weapons drops

##   Key link between SOE London and local receiver groups

## 

## \- MARIUS FIIL — owner of Hvidsten Inn (between Randers and Mariager)

##   Asked by Juncker to set up a receiver group of trustworthy locals

##   Leader of the Hvidsten Group

## 

## \- JENS TOLDSTRUP (real name Anton Ingersøn Jensen — different Jensen\!)

##   Leader of Danish Resistance Military Region 1

##   In charge of ALL reception groups for air supply drops to Jutland

##   Tax collector by trade — "Toldstrup" was cover name (play on "tolder")

##   Survived the war, visited SOE's Milton Hall June 1945

## 

## HOW THE CHAIN WORKED:

## 1\. LONDON sent coded message via BBC Danish Service

##    Signal: "Greetings to Elias — Listen again"

## 2\. That night: HALIFAX BOMBERS flew from England

##    Carried containers of explosives and weapons

## 3\. RECEIVER GROUPS collected drops at pre-arranged sites:

##    \- Mustard Point (near Hvidsten Inn)

##    \- Trinderup Heath (east of Mariager)

##    \- Overgaard Estate fields

## 4\. Weapons stored at KØSTERS BOGHANDEL

##    (bookshop in Randers, run by Otto Westergård Olesen)

##    Then distributed to sabotage groups across North Jutland

## 5\. SABOTAGE GROUPS carried out operations

## 

## THE LANGÅ EXPLOSIVES CHAIN:

## London → Halifax bomber → Hvidsten fields → Randers bookshop →

## Hoff's sabotage team → Langå bridges

## 

## THE CATASTROPHIC CHAIN REACTION (Dec 1943 — Oct 1944\)

## \------------------------------------------------------

## \- 13 Dec 1943: Jensen captured in Aarhus, reveals receiver networks

## \- 11 Mar 1944: Hvidsten Group arrested (8 later executed at Ryvangen)

## \- Mar/Apr 1944: Grethe Bartram (Aarhus communist/resistance circles)

##   hired as Gestapo informant — informs on \~50 more people

## \- Jun 1944: Samsing Group destroyed

## \- Oct 1944: Courier Ruth Phillipsen arrested, threatening entire Jutland leadership

## \- Result: By mid-1944, Jutland resistance IN RUINS

## 

## THE DESPERATE TELEGRAM:

## Resistance leader Vagn Bennike sent telegram to London:

## "The resistance in Jutland is about to be torn up by the Gestapo.

## I insistently ask that dormitories 4 and 5 may be destroyed by aerial attack."

## 

## This led directly to the AARHUS AIR RAID →

## 

## THE AARHUS AIR RAID — 31 OCTOBER 1944

## \--------------------------------------

## \- 25 RAF Mosquito fighter-bombers from 140 Wing, 2nd Tactical Air Force

## \- Target: Gestapo HQ at Aarhus University (dormitories 4 and 5\)

## \- Escorted by 12 Mustang fighters from 315 (Polish) Squadron

## \- Planned by SOE and American OSS together

## \- Challenge: civilian hospitals on BOTH SIDES of target — precision critical

## \- Pilots practised on 1:1 chalk layout before the raid

## \- Attack in 4 waves, 1 minute apart:

##   First 2 waves: regular bombs to blast buildings open

##   Last 2 waves: incendiary bombs to destroy archives

## \- Timed for 11:30am on a workday:

##   Danish prisoners would be back in cells for lunch

##   German staff would all be present

## \- RESULTS:

##   39 German agents and officers killed (27 SS/Gestapo including chief Schwitzgebel)

##   20 German soldiers killed at nearby barracks

##   Gestapo archives DESTROYED — files on Danish resistance gone

##   \~10 Danish civilians killed (builders working on university main building)

##   2 Danish prisoners present escaped in the confusion (Ruth Phillipsen \+ Harald Sandbæk)

##   1 Danish prisoner killed

## \- Called by RAF "the most successful mission of its kind during the war"

## \- 1 Mosquito damaged, limped to Sweden, crew destroyed it and were interned

## 

## NOTE: The Gestapo reinforced their Denmark numbers after the raid,

## nearly doubling their agent count. But the loss of archives and

## experienced personnel severely hampered their effectiveness.

## 

## THE PETER GROUP (PETERGRUPPEN) — GERMAN TERROR IN DENMARK

## \----------------------------------------------------------

## 

## WHY "PETER"?

## Named after its German leader's ALIAS. Otto Schwerdt used the cover name

## "Peter Schäfer" while operating in Denmark. Hence: the Peter Group.

## 

## OTTO SCHWERDT — THE MAN BEHIND IT:

## \- SS officer, born 1918 in Eisenberg, Germany

## \- Served in SS-Sonderverband z.b.V. Friedenthal under Otto Skorzeny

## \- Was SKORZENY'S SECOND-IN-COMMAND at the Gran Sasso raid

##   (the famous rescue of Mussolini, 12 September 1943\)

## \- Photo exists: Schwerdt at Mussolini's left shoulder, Skorzeny at right

## \- Awarded Deutsches Kreuz in Gold at ceremony in Berlin Sportpalast

## \- Himmler sent this high-status SS commando to Denmark specifically

##   to create a terror unit

## \- Led the Peter Group: December 1943 to November 1944

## \- Rose to rank of Hauptsturmführer

## 

## CREATION:

## \- Created late 1943 on orders of Heinrich Himmler

## \- Organised by SS Standartenfürer Otto Skorzeny

## \- Official name: "Sonderkommando Dänemark"

## \- Sole purpose: kill prominent Danes, perform terror operations

## \- Rule: For every German killed in Denmark, 5 Danish citizens killed

##   (Hitler wanted 10-for-1; Danish occupation command reduced it)

## 

## MEMBERS — A MIX OF GERMAN SS AND DANISH NAZIS:

## 

## Henning Brøndum:

## \- Danish Nazi, joined Waffen SS spring 1941

## \- Fought on Eastern Front against Russians

## \- National Museum: felt "intense feeling of contentment and sheer joy

##   of being alive" after attacks on Russians

## \- Brought that combat mindset back to Denmark

## \- Became one of most active Peter Group killers

## 

## Kai Henning Bothildsen Nielsen:

## \- Born Aarhus, 4 December 1919

## \- Dropped out of school at 16

## \- Joined Danish Nazi party (DNSAP) 1938

## \- Tried TWICE to join Waffen SS — rejected for medical reasons

## \- Ran a paint shop in Germany

## \- Joined Schalburg Corps intelligence wing

## \- Moved to Peter Group April 1944

## \- Codename: "PERLE" (Pearl)

## \- Quickly became one of the leaders

## 

## WHAT THEY DID:

## \- 94 MURDERS ("clearing murders" / clearingdrab)

## \- 25 attempted murders

## \- 157 sabotage events (against DANISH targets)

## \- 5 train bombings

## \- 3 robberies

## Total: 145 LIVES on their conscience

## 

## SPECIFIC ACTIONS:

## \- Kaj Munk (poet/playwright) — MURDERED 4 January 1944

##   (His poem now inscribed on Skæring Hede memorial stone)

## \- Four doctors murdered at Odense city/regional hospital — 20 February 1945

## \- Odinstårnet (Odin's Tower, Odense) BLOWN UP — 14 December 1944

##   (Denmark's tallest structure at the time)

## \- Cinemas, amusement parks, trains, trams, public buildings bombed

## \- Used CAPTURED SOE WEAPONS — including the Welrod silent pistol

##   (air-dropped to resistance but seized by Gestapo)

## 

## THE METHOD:

## \- Clearing murders done as STREET SHOOTINGS — maximise terror

## \- Aim: make Danish public BLAME THE RESISTANCE for the killings

## \- Doctors especially vulnerable — made house calls at all hours,

##   easy to ambush on doorsteps

## \- German newspapers forced to print resistance actions and

##   clearing murders SIDE BY SIDE on same page

## 

## AFTER THE WAR — JUSTICE:

## \- Bothildsen Nielsen: convicted of 57 murders, 9 attempted murders,

##   116 sabotage events. EXECUTED by firing squad, 03:15,

##   9 May 1947, Copenhagen. Age 27\.

##   (Attempted suicide when arrested 12 May 1945\)

## \- Henning Brøndum: sentenced to death, executed May 1947

## \- SEVEN Peter Group members total executed May 1947

## \- Otto Schwerdt: arrested, extradited to Denmark

##   Initially sentenced to DEATH

##   REDUCED to 24 years on appeal (Østre Landsret)

##   RELEASED 1 December 1953

##   Expelled from Denmark

##   Died in Cologne, 1975, age 56

##   THE MAN WHO CREATED THE WHOLE THING WALKED FREE

## 

## CONTEXT NOTE FROM FRANK:

## "There was a heck of a lot of resistance activity going on — hundreds of

## people involved. It adds credence to the fact that Denmark was an allied

## country, because people were fighting back, just like in France."

## 

## The Aarhus Air Raid connection: Frank noted he knew about the famous

## Mosquito precision raid but never knew it was linked to this story

## or that it was in Aarhus. The chain runs directly from the Langå

## sabotage through Jensen's capture to the bombing of Gestapo HQ.
